To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the likelihood of policy change is contingent on policy and geographical proximity.

(1) policy subsystems are more likely to respond to crises that are geographically and politically proximate to the policy subsystem; (2) the likelihood of policy change increases as a function of the number of crises that occur and their proximity to the policy subsystem.

(1) policy proximity and geographical proximity are key mechanisms linking external events to changes in policy subsystems, and (2) policy proximity is the key intervening variable linking geographical proximity to policy change.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the policy and geographical proximity of a crisis affects the prospects of policy change.
the question of why policy change occurs in a policy subsystem following a crisis and what the intervening mechanisms are that link the external event to the change process.
how external crises can affect policy change, and how this process varies across policy subsystems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the logic of policy change after crises is contingent on policy subsystems and their interaction with external events.
the impact of a crisis is contingent on the policy subsystem structure.
proximity and the interaction of the subsystems are the mechanisms linking disruptive crises to policy changes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the impact of crises on policy change is contingent on the policy subsystem structure and the type of crisis, with the latter being a function of geographical and policy proximity.
the proximity of a crisis to a subsystem and the structure of that subsystem determine the extent to which that crisis will be translated into policy change.
crises can be expected to trigger changes when the crisis is proximate to a subsystem, and the crisis has the capacity to change the policy subsystem's core values and beliefs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

crises can be conceptualized as a catalyst of policy change in a given policy subsystem, but that the extent of policy change is contingent on the structure of the subsystem and the type of crisis that is at stake.
policy proximity is the mechanism through which external events are translated into policy subsystem dynamics and, ultimately, policy change.
crises are not the sole cause of policy change.
